title: The Gradual Release of Responsibility in Action
author: Brendan Lee
summary: Brendan Lee, a former classroom teacher who now supports evidence-based instruction, unpacks the gradual release of responsibility (GRR) as more than a sequence of steps. He argues teachers need granular shared definitions because "my explicit instruction is not your explicit instruction." Using the Instructional Hierarchy, he says GRR fits the acquisition phase, when students are inaccurate, slow or unsure why an answer is right. In "I do" the teacher models briefly, since working memory is limited, and he warns against asking questions before the content has been taught. "We do" is the longest phase, with many questions, error correction and scaffolds such as sentence stems and example-problem pairs, and prompting fades gradually. "You do" must be genuinely independent and silent, and routines for it must be taught. He describes running multiple streams in one lesson and notes that practice is usually underestimated.
points: GRR should be used responsively, with the teacher moving between phases based on student responses rather than ticking off steps.
The Instructional Hierarchy tells teachers when to use GRR: while students are still in the acquisition phase and are not yet accurate.
The "I do" phase should be short (4 minutes in a 50 minute demo lesson) and should not include questions about content not yet taught.
"We do" is a cycle of modelling, practice and checking with fading prompts, supported by scaffolds like sentence stems and graphic organisers.
Independent practice must be truly independent, and teachers should expect to provide far more practice than they think is needed for mastery.
quotes: I’ve come to realise the importance of getting to the granular level of detail when it comes to defining our teaching practice. I’ve found that too often, we have discussions about concepts, but we’re actually talking about very different things e.g. “My explicit instruction is not your explicit instruction.

The GRR is not just a sequence of steps that you move through as a teacher, but it requires the teacher to move through the steps by acting responsively to the students based on the information they are giving you.
I try to not spend too much time in the “I do” phase because students will start to get restless and their working memory is limited. Explicit instruction is not lecturing.
Often, teachers can get the “I do” and “We do” phases mixed up by asking questions during the “I do” before we have actually taught them what we want them to know.

The ‘We Do’ phase is not just the teacher doing questions alongside of the students. Rather, it requires the teacher to go through a cycle of modelling, providing practice opportunities or checking for understanding and then gradually fading away the prompting and handing over more responsibility to the students.
Going off to Independent Practice is a routine that needs to be taught. My rule is that once they are there, they are working silently.
Often, we don’t provide students with enough practice activities because we underestimate how much practice it takes to reach mastery.
